title: ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
Consumer Price Index

Data
The series is CPIAUCSL, monthly and seasonally adjusted, from January 1947 to August 2023, 920 observations. It is modelled in logarithms so that differences are approximately percentage changes and the variance does not grow with the level.











Stationarity


Level                            ADF statistic  -0.82   p-value 0.960


Log level                        ADF statistic  -1.42   p-value 0.822


First difference of log          ADF statistic  -4.30   p-value < 0.01


Second difference of log         ADF statistic -15.04   p-value < 0.01


The level and the log level do not reject the unit root. The first difference of the log, which is monthly inflation, rejects it with a statistic of −4.30, but its ACF is significant at every one of the first 40 lags, with a lag-one value of 0.58 and a slow decline, and its PACF is significant through lag 7. Inflation is stationary by the test but so persistent that an ARMA model in first differences would need a high order to absorb the autocorrelation. The second difference has an ACF that cuts off after lag 2 (−0.31 and −0.16), apart from a cluster of small significant values at lags 10 to 12, and a PACF that tails off through lag 9. That pattern identifies a moving-average process of order 2. The model is therefore fitted with d = 2, which is also the order auto.arima selects.


















Model Selection
The grid covers p from 0 to 3 and q from 0 to 2 with d = 2, twelve models, all without a constant since a constant with d = 2 would impose a quadratic trend.

All coefficients in all three models are significant at the 5% level; the weakest is the third autoregressive term of ARIMA(3,2,2), with p = 0.047. The 80% interval at the end of the horizon runs from 311 to 466 and the 95% interval from 280 to 518, in index points.

Real GDP

Data
The series is GDPC1, quarterly, seasonally adjusted, from the first quarter of 1947 to the second quarter of 2023, 306 observations. It is modelled in logarithms.











Stationarity


Level                            ADF statistic  -1.05   p-value 0.929


Log level                        ADF statistic  -1.12   p-value 0.918


First difference of log          ADF statistic  -7.36   p-value < 0.01


Second difference of log         ADF statistic -11.30   p-value < 0.01


The first difference of log GDP, which is quarterly real growth, rejects the unit root with a statistic of −7.36. Its ACF is significant at lags 1 and 2 only, with a lag-one value of 0.13, and its PACF at lag 1 only. The mean of the differenced series is 0.0076 per quarter, 3.1% a year, so the model needs a drift term. A second difference is not required: its ACF has a lag-one value of −0.49, the signature of a series that has been differenced once too often. The models are fitted with d = 1 and drift.

title: ARMA, ARIMA and SARIMA Models
text:
3-Month Spread

Data
The series is T3MFF, the 3-month Treasury bill yield minus the effective Federal Funds Rate, daily from January 1982. The daily values are averaged within each calendar quarter, giving 168 quarters from the first quarter of 1982 to the fourth quarter of 2023. The final quarter contains only two trading days, 2 and 3 October 2023, and its value of 0.29 is the average of those two days. The quarterly series ranges from −1.49 points in the second quarter of 1982 to 0.55 in the third quarter of 2022, with a mean of −0.20. The mean is not stable across the sample: it is −0.62 over 1982–1989 and −0.10 from 1990 onward.











Stationarity


Level                            ADF statistic  -3.32   p-value 0.070


First difference                 ADF statistic  -7.29   p-value < 0.01


Level                            KPSS statistic   1.58   p-value < 0.01


Seasonal component range: -0.026 to 0.037 points. Series standard deviation: 0.333.


The evidence on the level is mixed at quarterly frequency. The ADF statistic is −3.32 with p = 0.070, a rejection at the 10% level but not at 5%; the KPSS test, whose null is stationarity, rejects with p below 0.01. On the daily data the ADF statistic is −8.28 and the unit root is rejected decisively (see the exploratory analysis). Averaging to quarters leaves 168 observations of a persistent series, and both tests have low power in that setting. The autocorrelation structure is unambiguous: the ACF declines geometrically, 0.82, 0.63, 0.47, 0.39, 0.35, and the PACF is significant at lag 1 only, at 0.82. That is the pattern of a stationary first-order autoregression, and a spread between two overnight-to-three-month rates is bounded by arbitrage, so it is modelled in levels.
Seasonality is negligible. The seasonal component from a classical decomposition ranges from −0.03 to +0.04 points against a standard deviation of 0.33, about a tenth of the variation. No seasonal differencing is applied; seasonal AR and MA terms are included in the grid so that the data can select them if they help.

The AR(1) coefficient is 0.844 with a standard error of 0.042, three and a half standard errors below one, and the mean is −0.204 with p = 0.019. The residual standard deviation is 0.183 points. The residuals have one autocorrelation outside the confidence band, −0.19 at lag 3, which puts the Ljung-Box p-values at lags 3 and 4 at 0.024 and 0.035; from lag 5 onward they exceed 0.05, reaching 0.14, 0.15 and 0.20 at lags 8, 12 and 20. Models that add a third lag, AR(3) and ARMA(1,3), remove the lag-3 autocorrelation but their additional coefficients are not significant and both have higher AIC and BIC than AR(1). The seasonal alternative has a seasonal AR coefficient of 0.79 and a seasonal MA coefficient of −0.86, which nearly cancel, and its Ljung-Box p-value at lag 8 is 0.026, worse than the simpler model. AR(1) is retained:
\[X_t - \mu = \phi\,(X_{t-1} - \mu) + w_t, \qquad \hat\phi = 0.844,\ \hat\mu = -0.204.\]

Model Choice
The four series divide into two groups by their order of integration, and the model that fits each group follows from that. CPI and real GDP are trending series that fail the unit root test in levels; the spreads are bounded series that pass it. The two trending series are modelled in differences and the two spreads in levels, and in every case BIC chose the smallest model in the grid that the diagnostics could support.
For CPI the retained model is ARIMA(0,2,2) on the log index. The second difference is used because monthly inflation, the first difference, is stationary by the ADF test but autocorrelated at every lag out to 40; a model in first differences would have needed a high order to absorb that. The two moving-average coefficients, −0.56 and −0.25, make the model equivalent to Holt’s linear-trend method, so its forecast extends the level and slope estimated at the end of the sample. That slope reflects the inflation of 2021–2023 and produces a five-year path of 4.4% a year, above the 3.7% recorded over the twelve months to August 2023.
For real GDP the retained model is ARIMA(1,1,0) with drift on the log level. Quarterly real growth is stationary with a lag-one autocorrelation of 0.13 and no structure beyond lag 2, so a random walk with drift and one autoregressive correction is sufficient. The drift, 0.0076 per quarter, is 3.1% a year, and the forecast grows at that rate. This model replaced the ARIMA(1,1,1) that a grid restricted to q = 1 would have selected; the moving-average term in that model had p = 0.16 and its removal lowers every information criterion.
For both spreads the retained model is AR(1) with a mean. The ACF declines geometrically and the PACF cuts off at lag 1 in both series, and BIC prefers AR(1) over every larger model by more than three points. The autoregressive coefficients, 0.84 for the 3-month spread and 0.74 for the 6-month, give half-lives of 4.1 and 2.3 quarters: a shock to the 3-month spread takes about a year to decay by half, and a shock to the 6-month spread about seven months. The 6-month spread’s mean is not distinguishable from zero. Seasonal terms were offered to the grid and did not survive: where they enter the AIC-minimising models they appear as near-cancelling pairs, and the seasonal component from a classical decomposition is a tenth of the series’ standard deviation.


Residual Diagnostics
Three of the four retained models have residuals that pass the Ljung-Box test at every lag examined. The exception is CPI, whose residuals fail at lags 12 and 20 with p-values below 0.001 because of autocorrelation at lags 10 to 12. The series is published seasonally adjusted, but the adjustment leaves a small annual pattern in the second difference. auto.arima’s seasonal model, SARIMA(1,2,1)(2,0,0)[12], reduces the problem but does not remove it, and was not retained because the gain does not justify three additional parameters for a pattern this small. The 3-month spread’s AR(1) has one significant residual autocorrelation at lag 3, −0.19, which no model in the grid removes without adding insignificant coefficients. Residuals of both spread models are heavier-tailed than normal, with the largest values in 1982 and 2008, so the prediction intervals understate the tails.


Forecast Accuracy
Against the benchmark methods on the training set, the retained model has the lowest RMSE for all four series. The margins differ. For CPI the model’s RMSE is 60% of the naive method’s and 80% of the drift method’s. For GDP the model and the drift method are within 1% of each other, which is expected since the model is a drift model with a small correction. For the spreads the model’s RMSE is 4% and 7% below the naive method’s, a small margin, and the mean-percentage measures are not informative because both series cross zero.
The rolling-origin cross-validation on the spreads gives the only out-of-sample evidence. For the 6-month spread AR(1) has the lowest error at every horizon from one to four quarters, with a one-step MAE of 0.116 points. For the 3-month spread AR(1) is competitive one step ahead, with a mean squared error of 0.0197 against 0.0195 for the best alternative, but at four quarters ahead its MAE of 0.212 is above the 0.156 of a differenced SARIMA(1,1,1)(2,1,1)[4]. The cause is a shift in the spread’s mean, from −0.62 over 1982–1989 to −0.10 since 1990, which a constant-mean model cannot accommodate: every forecast is pulled toward a mean estimated from a sample that includes the 1980s. The differenced model avoids that by carrying the current level forward, but it does so through a moving-average coefficient of −1.00, which is the estimator undoing the differencing, and its residuals fail the Ljung-Box test at lag 8. The AR(1) is retained as the correctly identified model, with the caveat that its multi-quarter forecasts for the 3-month spread would be improved by a mean estimated on the post-1990 sample or by a model that allows the mean to shift.


Limitations
All four models are univariate. They describe how each series moves relative to its own past and say nothing about the Federal Funds Rate, which is the variable this project is about. The ARIMAX section that follows adds the policy rate as a regressor. Three further limits apply. The GDP forecast runs fifteen years, far beyond the horizon at which a univariate model is informative; it reports the sample’s average growth rate, not a projection of the economy. The CPI forecast inherits the 2021–2023 slope and should be read as a continuation of recent inflation rather than an expectation about it. And the final quarterly observation for both spreads is an average of two trading days, 2 and 3 October 2023, which adds noise to the last point the models fit and forecast from.

The test period is the last 15% of the sample, the 82 months from October 2016 to July 2023, shaded in the figure. title: Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
Design


Window length 12 months. Training samples 453 (of which 67 held out for early stopping), test samples 82.


Each training sample is a window of the twelve previous months and the target is the following month, so consecutive samples overlap by eleven months and the 465 training months yield 453 samples. The series are standardised with the mean and standard deviation of the training period only, so that no information from the test period enters the model. Each network has one recurrent layer of 32 units followed by a linear output, giving 1,121 parameters for the RNN, 4,385 for the LSTM and 3,393 for the GRU in the univariate version, and slightly more with the second input. Training minimises mean squared error with the Adam optimiser at a learning rate of 0.001 in batches of 32, for up to 300 epochs, and stops when the loss on the last 15% of the training samples has not improved for 15 epochs, restoring the weights from the best epoch. Forecasts are one step ahead on the test windows, without re-estimation. Errors are reported in index points after reversing the standardisation.

title: Deep Learning for Time Series
text:
Deep Learning and Linear Models
On this series the recurrent networks match the linear models and do not improve on them. Three features of the problem explain that. The sample is small by the standards of deep learning, 453 training windows, so a network with one to four thousand parameters is estimated from fewer examples than it has weights, and early stopping at 50 to 180 epochs is what prevents it from fitting the training set. The series is nearly a random walk at monthly frequency, so the best one-step forecast is close to the last value and there is little nonlinear structure for a network to find; the ARIMA’s advantage comes from a linear correction the networks could represent but do not learn reliably. And the test period contains a shock, the pandemic, whose size has no precedent in the training data, which penalises every method equally.
The networks also cost more to use. Each requires a choice of window length, units, optimiser, learning rate, batch size and stopping rule, and its result varies with the seed by up to 0.08 points of RMSE; the ARIMA is specified by three integers chosen by AIC and is the same every time. The RNN, the simplest network, is the best of the three here and the one whose training is fastest, which is consistent with the data supporting only a small amount of structure. Where recurrent networks earn their cost is on long, high-frequency series with nonlinear dynamics or many inputs; a 547-month survey index is not that case.
The policy rate does not help either model class predict sentiment a month ahead. This is consistent with the ARIMAX finding for inflation: the policy rate’s effect on households operates through channels, credit conditions, employment, prices, that take longer than a month and that a direct regression on the rate does not capture.

What the Section Found
Consumer sentiment is a persistent series whose month-to-month changes are close to unpredictable, and every method tested, from the naive forecast to a 4,500-parameter LSTM, produces one-step-ahead errors of about 4.5 index points on the 2016–2023 test period. The ordering is naive ≈ networks > ARIMA by margins of 1 to 2%, with the ARIMA’s advantage coming from a small mean-reversion term. At twelve months the RNN is marginally the best, 6% below the naive forecast. No difference in this section is statistically distinguishable from zero.
The Federal Funds Rate has no predictive value for sentiment at a one-month horizon. It lowers the ARIMA’s RMSE by 0.3% and raises the RNN’s and LSTM’s by 3 to 4%; its correlation with sentiment is −0.04 in levels and 0.03 in changes. This is the third section of the study to find that the policy rate’s contemporaneous or short-lag relationship with a target is weak or absent, after the inflation regression and the dollar-return equation, and the same reason applies: the rate responds to the economy and acts on it with a lag.


Model Choice
For this series the linear models are the right tool and the networks are a check on them. A recurrent network is a flexible function of the last twelve observations, and on a series where the best forecast is close to the last observation the flexibility is not used. The comparison is fair to the networks, with standardisation by training statistics, early stopping on a held-out set, five seeds and a deterministic configuration, and it would need a longer or richer series to come out differently. If the study were extended, a network with inputs beyond sentiment and the policy rate, such as unemployment, inflation and equity returns, would be the natural next test, since the multivariate case is where recurrent networks have an architectural advantage over ARIMAX.


Limitations
The test period is 82 months and includes one extreme event, so the RMSE ranking is sensitive to a few observations; a Diebold-Mariano test rejects none of the differences. The networks were tuned only lightly, with one architecture, one window length and one learning rate, and a search over those settings could change the margins, though not, on this evidence, the conclusion. The recursive multi-step forecasts of the networks use the seed-0 models only. The ARIMA order was chosen once on the training period and held fixed while the coefficients were re-estimated each month; the networks were not re-estimated during the test period, which favours the ARIMA slightly at the one-step horizon.

Both models pass every test on the standardised residuals: no autocorrelation in the residuals or their squares at lags 10 or 20, and no remaining ARCH effect (LM p-values of 0.91 and 0.97). The standardised residuals have kurtosis of about 5, which the Student-t with 7.4 to 7.6 degrees of freedom accommodates. The models differ on asymmetry. In the symmetric model the negative-sign-bias test rejects at p = 0.018: the variance responds to the sign of the previous innovation in a way the model does not capture. The GJR model’s asymmetry coefficient is −0.036 with a standard error of 0.008, the likelihood-ratio test rejects the symmetric model with p < 0.001, and the sign-bias tests no longer reject jointly (p = 0.27).
The sign of the asymmetry is the reverse of what is found in equity markets. In the GJR model the coefficient on a squared innovation is \(\alpha\) when the innovation is positive and \(\alpha + \gamma\) when it is negative. Here \(\alpha = 0.058\) and \(\gamma = -0.036\), so a positive innovation, a rise in the dollar, adds 0.058 times its square to next day’s variance, and a fall in the dollar adds 0.022 times its square. Dollar appreciations are the larger source of volatility. This fits the dollar’s role in the sample: it rises when investors leave riskier assets, in the autumn of 2008, in the spring of 2020 and during 2022, and those are the periods in which its volatility is highest.
The retained model, with \(r_t\) the daily log return in %, \(\varepsilon_t\) the innovation, \(\sigma_t^2\) its conditional variance and \(I_{t-1} = 1\) when \(\varepsilon_{t-1} < 0\), is
\[r_t = -0.0001 + 0.039\, r_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t, \qquad \varepsilon_t = \sigma_t z_t, \quad z_t \sim t_{7.6},\]
\[\sigma_t^2 = 0.0005 + \left(0.058 - 0.036\, I_{t-1}\right)\varepsilon_{t-1}^2 + 0.956\, \sigma_{t-1}^2.\]
Persistence is 0.9955, so half of a shock to the variance remains after 155 trading days. The unconditional daily standard deviation implied by the model is 0.34%.

Realised volatility is the square root of the sum of squared daily returns within the month, in %; its mean is 1.45% and its median 1.34%. Three facts stand out. First, volatility is higher in months when the policy rate moves: 1.50% on average in the 160 months with any change against 1.29% in the 52 with none, a difference the t-test puts at p = 0.014, and the correlation with the absolute change is 0.40. Second, the direction matters. Months in which the rate was cut have the highest volatility, 1.91% on average across 20 months, against 1.48% in the 40 months it was raised and 1.38% when it was unchanged. The cuts are concentrated in 2007–2008 and March 2020, the two periods of financial stress in the sample, so this is the Federal Reserve responding to the conditions that also move the dollar rather than the cuts causing the volatility. Cut months also have the highest average dollar return, 0.34%, which is the safe-haven appreciation of those periods. Third, the level of the rate is negatively related to volatility: a rate one point higher is associated with realised volatility 3.5% lower once the month’s change and last month’s volatility are held fixed, and 8% lower without those controls. The low-rate years include 2008–2009 and 2020, and the high-rate years 2006–2007 and 2023, which were calm.
The regressions confirm that the size of the month’s move is the stronger of the two: in the fullest specification a one-point absolute change raises log realised volatility by 0.60, a factor of 1.8, with p below 0.001, alongside a lagged-volatility coefficient of 0.62 that carries the persistence the GARCH model captures at daily frequency. The Granger tests give the direction. The change in the policy rate does not help predict next month’s volatility at any lag order, with p-values of 0.39 to 0.74, while volatility does help predict the next change in the rate, with p = 0.002 at two lags and 0.008 at three. The sequence is the same one the vector autoregression on the yield curve found: market conditions lead, the policy rate follows. A month of high dollar volatility is a signal that the Federal Reserve is more likely to move the rate in the following months, in the sample mostly to cut it.
Two qualifications apply. The monthly average rate is not a measure of policy surprises; a rate change that was fully anticipated moves the dollar little on the day it is made, and the measure used here does not distinguish anticipated from unanticipated moves. And the daily-frequency effect, while statistically supported, is modest against the model’s own dynamics: a 0.25-point month adds about 6% to the conditional standard deviation, whereas the 2008 crisis tripled it.

Regression of log RV on |change in FFR| and FFR level, 120 months, R² = 0.27: |change| 1.86 (s.e. 0.28, p < 0.001); level -0.057 (s.e. 0.033, p 0.088).


The relationship found for the dollar holds for the stock market and is stronger. Over the 120 months from October 2013 to August 2023, monthly realised volatility averages 3.6% in the 81 months the policy rate was unchanged, 4.9% in the 33 months it was raised and 9.0% in the six months it was cut; the cuts are the 2019 easing and March–April 2020. The correlation between realised volatility and the size of the month’s rate change is 0.65, against 0.40 for the dollar, and in the regression a one-point change is associated with log volatility 1.86 higher, a factor of 6.4, with p below 0.001, while the level of the rate has no significant effect. The stock market, like the dollar, is most volatile in the months the Federal Reserve moves, and most of all when it cuts, because the cuts come in the episodes of financial stress that also drive equity volatility.

text:
Summary

AR(1), coefficient 0.039

GJR-GARCH(1,1): ω = 0.0005, α = 0.058, γ = −0.036, β = 0.956

Student-t, 7.6 degrees of freedom


Persistence
0.9955; half-life 155 trading days

Dollar appreciations add 0.058 × ε² to variance, depreciations 0.022 × ε²


Residual tests
No autocorrelation in z or z², no remaining ARCH effect, no sign bias


Out-of-sample rank
Lowest MSE and QLIKE of six methods over 1,346 days


VaR coverage
1% and 5% exceedance rates as expected


Federal Funds Rate
|Change in FFR| significant in the variance equation (LR p = 0.012); level not; volatility Granger-causes FFR changes, not the reverse


S&P 500
AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) normal: α = 0.203, β = 0.769, persistence 0.971; residual tests pass; monthly RV correlation 0.65 with |ΔFFR|






What the Model Found
Dollar returns are unpredictable in sign and predictable in size. The mean equation explains almost nothing, an autocorrelation of 0.04, while the variance equation is strongly supported: an ARCH-LM statistic of 548 in the raw returns and none in the model’s residuals. The variance is persistent, with a coefficient on lagged variance of 0.956 and a half-life of half a trading year, and heavy-tailed, with innovations that follow a t-distribution with about 7.6 degrees of freedom. The two additions to a basic GARCH(1,1) that the data support are the heavy-tailed distribution, worth 93 log-likelihood points, and asymmetry, worth 10. The asymmetry runs opposite to the leverage effect in equities: rises in the dollar raise its volatility more than falls do, which is consistent with the dollar strengthening during flights to safety.
The volatility path reproduces the episodes documented elsewhere on this site. The financial crisis of 2008 produced a peak three times the median and the highest readings in the sample; the pandemic produced the second-highest; the euro-area crisis, the Brexit vote and the 2022–2023 tightening each produced peaks of about 0.5 to 0.57% a day. Between 2012 and 2019 the dollar was quiet.


Forecasting
The model’s advantage over simpler methods is real but modest. Over the last 1,346 days its one-day variance forecasts beat the RiskMetrics EWMA by 0.02 on QLIKE and a 22-day rolling variance by 0.06, and its value-at-risk quantiles are exceeded at the right frequency. A practitioner who needs a daily volatility estimate for the dollar would lose little with the EWMA and would lose noticeably with a constant variance. The 60-day forecast is a slow drift from 0.32% to 0.33% a day; GARCH forecasts are informative about the level of volatility over the next few weeks and, beyond the half-life, converge to the unconditional level.


The S&P 500
The stock market shows the same structure with larger numbers. An AR(1)-GARCH(1,1) model estimated with fGarch passes the Ljung-Box and LM ARCH tests on its standardised residuals; its ARCH coefficient is 0.20 and its persistence 0.97, so equity volatility reacts to a shock three and a half times as strongly as the dollar’s and forgets it six times as fast, with a half-life of 24 days. The March 2020 peak, 7.9% a day, is ten times the median. Monthly equity volatility is 0.65 correlated with the size of the month’s policy-rate change, 35% higher in months the rate is raised and two and a half times higher in months it is cut.


The Federal Funds Rate
The policy rate enters the dollar’s volatility through the size of its moves, not its level. At daily frequency the absolute change in the month’s rate is a significant variance regressor (likelihood-ratio p = 0.012), raising the conditional standard deviation by about 6% in a month with a 0.25-point move; the rate level has a coefficient of zero. At monthly frequency realised volatility is 16% higher in months the rate changes than in months it does not, 48% higher in months it is cut, and a one-point move is associated with volatility 1.8 times higher after controlling for the previous month. The timing is the same as in the yield-curve VAR: dollar volatility Granger-causes changes in the policy rate (p = 0.002), and changes in the policy rate do not Granger-cause dollar volatility. The Federal Reserve moves the rate in the months after the dollar market has become volatile, in this sample most often by cutting into a period of stress, and the moves themselves add a modest amount to volatility while they are being made. A test with a daily measure of policy surprises, which this data set does not contain, would separate the two more sharply.


Limitations
The squared return is a noisy proxy for the variance, and the out-of-sample comparison inherits that noise; realised variance from intraday data would give sharper rankings. The sample contains two regime changes, the 2008 crisis and the 2020 pandemic, and a model with constant parameters fitted across both estimates an average of their dynamics; the rolling re-estimation in the out-of-sample exercise partly addresses this. The Student-t distribution is symmetric, and the skewed-t did not improve on it, so the asymmetry in the data is carried entirely by the variance equation. The mean equation’s residuals retain small autocorrelations at lags 8 to 20 which are not modelled. The policy-rate variable is a monthly average assigned to every day of its month, so the daily variance regressor is a step function and the monthly analysis cannot distinguish a rate change made at the start of a month from one made at the end.

title: Introduction
text:
Fed Funds Rate transmission map 





 Grey — policy instrument (Fed Funds Rate, government spending)
 Blue — market rates and transmission channels
 Green — leading indicators (turn 3–12 months before the economy)
 Yellow — coincident indicators (move with the economy)
 Red — lagging indicators (turn after the economy)
Thick arrows — strongest channels
Dotted arrows — leading indicators feeding into GDP





Statement of Purpose
This project examines how changes in the Federal Funds Rate pass through to other parts of the U.S. economy. The series covered are Treasury yields and spreads across the curve, real GDP, CPI inflation, the unemployment rate, the 30-year mortgage rate, the U.S. dollar index, the S&P 500, and consumer sentiment. This page describes the channels involved; the map above includes nodes such as jobless claims and building permits that place the modelled series in context but are not themselves modelled. Later sections test the channels with time series models: univariate ARMA models, regressions and vector autoregressions with the Federal Funds Rate, a GARCH model of dollar volatility, and recurrent neural networks.
The starting point is the Harvard Law Review (2023) note on the Federal Reserve’s rate increase of March 22, 2023, Federal Reserve — U.S. Monetary Policy Shows the Major Issues with the Major Questions Doctrine



Central Bank
A central bank is the institution responsible for a country’s monetary policy. In the United States this is the Federal Reserve System. Other examples are the Bank of England and the European Central Bank. The main tools are the policy interest rate, the size of the balance sheet, and guidance about future policy. Because the dollar is the main funding and reserve currency, Federal Reserve decisions also affect borrowing costs and exchange rates outside the United States.


Interest Rate
The policy rate is the central bank’s primary tool. A higher rate raises the cost of borrowing for households and firms. Consumption and investment slow, and GDP growth slows with them. Inflation responds later, usually with a lag of a year or more. A lower rate works in the opposite direction.


Fed Funds Rate
The Federal Funds Rate is the overnight rate at which banks lend reserves to each other. The Federal Open Market Committee sets a target range for it at eight scheduled meetings a year. It is the shortest rate in the economy and the anchor for the rest of the yield curve. Bills maturing within a year track it closely. Longer maturities respond less directly, since their yields also reflect expected future policy, expected inflation, and a term premium. Longer-term yields in turn set borrowing costs for mortgages and corporate debt and the discount rate applied to equities.



Gross Domestic Product
GDP is the sum of consumption, investment, government spending, and net exports. Consumption is roughly two-thirds of the total. Rate changes reach GDP mainly through investment (housing and business capital spending) and consumption (credit costs and the wealth effect from asset prices). Net exports respond through the exchange rate: higher U.S. rates relative to other countries strengthen the dollar, which makes imports cheaper and exports more expensive.
GDP is a coincident indicator. It is published quarterly, about a month after the quarter ends, and is revised for several years afterward.


Risk-Free Rate
The risk-free rate is the return on an asset with no default risk. In practice U.S. Treasury yields are used, with the maturity matched to the horizon in question: the 3-month bill for short horizons and the 10-year note for longer ones. The rate is nominal and therefore includes expected inflation. The real risk-free rate is observed from Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities (TIPS). LIBOR served as the short-term benchmark for decades but was discontinued in June 2023 and replaced by SOFR, which is based on overnight Treasury repo transactions.


U.S. Treasury Securities
The Treasury issues three types of marketable debt. Bills mature in 4 to 52 weeks, are sold at a discount, and pay no coupon. Notes mature in 2, 3, 5, 7, or 10 years. Bonds mature in 20 or 30 years. Notes and bonds pay interest semi-annually. All three are backed by the full faith and credit of the U.S. government and are treated as free of default risk. The Treasury market is the largest and most liquid bond market in the world, and its yields serve as reference rates for most other dollar borrowing. The 10-year note is the most widely quoted. The 30-year mortgage rate, for example, is priced as a spread over the 10-year yield rather than over the 30-year bond, because most mortgages are repaid or refinanced well before maturity.


Treasury Yield Curve
The yield curve plots Treasury yields against maturity on a given day. It normally slopes upward, since investors require more yield to lend for longer. The slope is usually summarized as a spread, most often the 10-year yield minus the 2-year yield or the 10-year minus the 3-month. An inverted curve, where short yields exceed long yields, has preceded every U.S. recession since the late 1960s, typically by 6 to 18 months. This makes the spread one of the most closely watched leading indicators. The Federal Funds Rate sets the short end of the curve directly. The long end is set by the market.

U.S. Department of Treasury (2026)


Summary
The Federal Reserve sets the Federal Funds Rate. Short-maturity Treasury yields follow it closely, and long-maturity yields follow it partially, adjusted for expectations and term premium. Those yields set borrowing costs across the economy, and borrowing costs move investment, consumption, asset prices, and the exchange rate. Employment and inflation respond last. Since the Fed’s mandate variables are lagging indicators, the Fed relies on leading indicators such as the yield curve spread, equity prices, and jobless claims to judge where the economy is heading. The remaining sections of this project test these relationships in the data.







References

Harvard Law Review. 2023. Federal Reserve Interest Rate Hike on March 22, 2023. 136 (7): 2028–35. https://harvardlawreview.org/print/vol-136/federal-reserve-interest-rate-hike-on-march-22-2023/.


U.S. Department of Treasury. 2026. Daily Treasury Rates. Https://home.treasury.gov/resource-center/data-chart-center/interest-rates/TextView?type=daily_treasury_yield_curve.

title: Data Visualization
text:
Short-Term Spreads
The three series in this section are spreads: the 3-month, 6-month, and 1-year Treasury yields minus the effective Federal Funds Rate on the same day, in % points. The Federal Funds Rate is the rate the Fed controls. A Treasury bill yield is the rate the market sets for lending to the government over the same horizon. The difference between them is a direct reading of where the market expects policy to go.
A bill yield below the Federal Funds Rate means investors accept less than the current policy rate to lock in a return for the next few months, which they do when they expect the Fed to cut. A bill yield above it means they demand more, which they do when they expect the Fed to raise. The spread turns negative before easing cycles and positive before tightening cycles. The 1-year spread moves first and furthest, since it has the most room to price in future changes.


                            
                                            



The three lines keep their order. Over 1982–2023 the 3-month spread averages −0.21 points, the 6-month −0.03, and the 1-year +0.13. The 3-month bill usually yields slightly less than the Federal Funds Rate because it is the safest and most liquid instrument in the market, while a Federal Funds loan is an unsecured overnight loan between banks. The 1-year sits above because it carries a year of expected rate changes and a small term premium.
The spread turns negative ahead of each easing cycle. Sustained negative readings appear in 1988–90 before the 1990 recession, through 1997–98 during the Asian and Russian crises, in 2000–01 before the dot-com recession, from mid-2006 through 2008 before and during the financial crisis, in mid-2019 before the Fed’s first cuts since 2008, and briefly in March 2020 at the onset of the pandemic. Sustained positive readings are rarer, since the 3-month bill normally sits below the policy rate. They appear in 2018 and through 2022, when the market priced in the Fed’s hiking cycles. From 2009 to 2015 the 3-month spread stays within two tenths of a point of zero, since both the bill yield and the Federal Funds Rate were held near zero, while the 6-month and 1-year spreads drift above it as the market priced in an eventual lift-off.
The largest readings are artifacts. On the last trading day of 1985 and 1986 the effective Federal Funds Rate spiked as banks bid for reserves over the year-end, pushing the 3-month spread to −6 and −10 points for a day or two. The vertical axis is clipped at −6 so that these two days do not compress the rest of the series. The range slider below the chart can be used to zoom in on any period.



Long-Maturity Yields and the Mortgage Rate
The long end of the curve is shown as yields, not spreads. The 10-year, 20-year, and 30-year constant-maturity yields are plotted with the 30-year fixed mortgage rate, all in %. The 20-year line breaks between 1987 and 1993, the years in which the Treasury did not publish a 20-year constant-maturity yield.


                            
                                            


The four lines are close to a single line. Pairwise correlations between the three Treasury yields and the mortgage rate are all above 0.97. The 10-year yield peaked at 15.8% in September 1981, fell for four decades to a low of 0.5% in August 2020, and rose to 4.8% by October 2023. The mortgage rate follows the 10-year yield with an average gap of 1.7 % points, which is the lender’s compensation for prepayment risk and servicing. The gap widens when rates are volatile, as in 2008 and 2022, and narrows when they are stable.


Rates and the Economy
The last chart places the Federal Funds Rate and the mortgage rate alongside four measures of the economy. CPI and real GDP are levels that rise through the whole sample, so they are shown as year-over-year % changes: inflation and growth. The dollar index is shown the same way, as its year-over-year change, using the series that begins in 2006. The unemployment rate is used as published. Every line is then in % and shares one axis.


                            
                                            



The inflation of the 1970s and its end. Inflation reached 12.2% in November 1974 and 14.6% in March 1980. The Fed’s response under Paul Volcker took the Federal Funds Rate to 19.1% in June 1981, more than nine points above inflation and the highest real policy rate in the sample. The mortgage rate followed to 18.6% that October. Inflation was below 4% by the end of 1982 and stayed low for four decades. The cost was two recessions and an unemployment rate of 10.8% in November 1982.
The shape of every cycle since. The Federal Funds Rate rises during an expansion, unemployment falls, and growth runs between 2 and 4% in most quarters. The Fed cuts as growth slows, and unemployment rises after the cuts begin: 7.8% in 1992, 6.3% in 2003, and 10.0% in 2009. The 2008 recession is the one case where inflation turned negative, at −2.0% in July 2009, and the Federal Funds Rate was then held near zero for seven years. The dollar index rose 21.7% year over year in March 2009 as investors moved into dollars during the crisis, which shows that the dollar responds to risk as well as to rate differentials.
The pandemic. Real GDP fell 7.5% year over year in the second quarter of 2020 and rose 12.0% a year later, the largest swings in the sample, and unemployment jumped to 14.7% in April 2020. Inflation followed, reaching 8.9% in June 2022 while the Federal Funds Rate was still 0.2%, a real policy rate of −8.3 points in March 2022 and the lowest in the sample. The Fed raised the rate above 5% within sixteen months. The dollar index rose 12.9% year over year in October 2022 as U.S. rates climbed faster than rates abroad, the rate-differential channel from the introduction.

title: Exploratory Data Analysis
text:
Purpose
This section examines each series before any model is fitted. For each one it shows four things: the series over time, its autocorrelation function (ACF), its partial autocorrelation function (PACF), and the ACF of its first difference. It then applies the augmented Dickey-Fuller test to the level and to the first difference.
The question these tools answer is whether a series is stationary. A stationary series has a constant mean and variance and an autocorrelation that depends only on the lag, so its past behaviour is informative about its future. A series with a unit root does not revert to a mean and must be differenced before it can be modelled with ARMA methods. The answer determines the order of differencing used in the sections that follow.
Twelve series are examined: the three short-term spreads, the three long-maturity yields, and six economic series. The 5-year spread is used only in the ARIMAX section and consumer sentiment only in the deep learning section, so they are examined there. Each series is read from its own source file, described on the data source page, and analysed over its full available sample.


Stationarity
The augmented Dickey-Fuller test (Dickey and Fuller 1979) tests the null hypothesis that a series has a unit root against the alternative that it is stationary around a linear trend. The implementation is adf.test from the tseries package (Trapletti and Hornik 2026), which fits a regression with a constant and a linear trend and sets the lag order to the integer part of \((n-1)^{1/3}\). Its p-values are interpolated from the tables in Banerjee et al. (1993) and are reported only within the range 0.01 to 0.99, so a value shown as “< 0.01” is at the lower bound. A p-value below 0.05 rejects the unit root at the 5% level. The table reports the test statistic and p-value for the level of each series and for its first difference.

The results divide the series into two groups. The three spreads reject the unit root in levels, with test statistics between −7.6 and −9.0. They are stationary and can be modelled without differencing. This is expected: a spread between two rates that move together is bounded. The ARMA section models quarterly averages of the 3-month and 6-month spreads.
Eight of the remaining nine series do not reject the unit root in levels at the 5% level, and every series rejects it after a single difference, with statistics between −5.4 and −22.8 among those eight. They are integrated of order one and enter the models in first differences. Three results deserve comment. The 30-year yield and the Federal Funds Rate have p-values of 0.088 and 0.091, so they reject at the 10% level but not at 5%; both are treated as I(1). The unemployment rate rejects at the 5% level, with p = 0.013, on the full sample from 1948. Unemployment is bounded and reverts toward a long-run level, so the result is plausible, but the series is highly persistent, with an autocorrelation above 0.5 out to 16 months, and it is differenced in the sections that use it. CPI rejects the unit root after one difference, but the differenced series is itself strongly autocorrelated, with a lag-one coefficient of 0.59, which is why the ARMA section fits the logarithm of the index with a second difference.
Every level series apart from the spreads has a first-order autocorrelation above 0.96. Their ACF plots below decay so slowly that the bars remain near one across the entire plotted range, which is the visual signature of a unit root. The ACF of the first difference, in the lower-right panel of each figure, is the plot that carries information about the model order.


Treasury Series

T3MFFT6MFFT1YFFDGS10DGS20DGS30











The 3-month spread runs daily from January 1982 to October 2023, 10,442 observations. It ranges from −10.32 points on 30 December 1986 to 1.98 points on 24 October 1984, and its mean is −0.21. The low is a single-day year-end spike in the effective Federal Funds Rate, discussed on the visualization page. The ADF statistic in levels is −8.28, which rejects the unit root. The ACF starts at 0.83 and falls below 0.5 within 44 trading days, about two months, so shocks to the spread fade within a quarter. The PACF has a large first spike and small values after it. The first difference has a lag-one autocorrelation of −0.20, the negative value that results from differencing a stationary series.











The 6-month spread covers the same sample. Its range is −10.24 to 2.37 points, with both extremes on the same days as the 3-month spread, and its mean is −0.03. The ADF statistic is −7.60 and the unit root is rejected. The ACF starts at 0.83 and falls below 0.5 within 35 trading days. The lag-one autocorrelation of the first difference is −0.20. The 6-month spread behaves as the 3-month spread does, with slightly faster decay.











The 1-year spread has the longest sample of the three, daily from January 1962 to October 2023, 15,423 observations. It ranges from −10.11 points, again on 30 December 1986, to 3.61 points on 8 December 1965, and its mean is 0.04. The ADF statistic in levels is −8.96 and the unit root is rejected. Its autocorrelation decays most slowly of the three: the ACF starts at 0.89 and does not fall below 0.5 until lag 64, about three months. The longer horizon leaves more room for expected rate changes to accumulate, so the spread moves in longer swings. The first difference has a lag-one autocorrelation of −0.27.











The 10-year yield runs daily from January 1962 to October 2023, 15,425 observations. It peaked at 15.84% on 30 September 1981 and reached its low of 0.52% on 4 August 2020. The ADF statistic in levels is −2.36 with p = 0.43, so the unit root is not rejected. The ACF at lag one is 0.9997 and does not fall below 0.5 until lag 1,887, about seven and a half years. After one difference the statistic is −22.85 and the unit root is rejected. The differenced series has a lag-one autocorrelation of 0.06, close to white noise, which is what a random walk implies for daily yield changes.











The 20-year series has a gap. The Treasury discontinued the 20-year constant-maturity yield at the end of 1986 and reinstated it on 1 October 1993, so the level plot is blank for those years. Joining the two segments end to end would produce a false jump and a compressed time axis, so the autocorrelation plots and the test use only the continuous segment from October 1993, 7,507 observations. Over that period the yield ranges from 8.30% on 4 November 1994 to 0.87% on 9 March 2020. The ADF statistic is −1.95 with p = 0.60 in levels and −17.60 after one difference. The lag-one autocorrelation of the first difference is −0.01.











The 30-year yield runs from February 1977 to October 2023, 11,655 observations, from a peak of 15.21% on 26 October 1981 to a low of 0.99% on 9 March 2020. The ADF statistic in levels is −3.20 with p = 0.088, which rejects at 10% but not at 5%. Given a lag-one autocorrelation of 0.9997 and an ACF that does not fall below 0.5 until lag 1,685, the series is treated as I(1). After one difference the statistic is −20.60 and the lag-one autocorrelation is 0.03.





Economic Series

MORTGAGE30USFEDFUNDSCPIAUCSLUNRATEGDPC1DTWEXBGS











The 30-year mortgage rate is weekly, from April 1971 to September 2023, 2,740 observations. It peaked at 18.63% on 9 October 1981 and reached its low of 2.65% on 7 January 2021. The ADF statistic in levels is −2.18 with p = 0.50. The ACF does not fall below 0.5 until lag 364, seven years. After one difference the statistic is −14.02. Unlike the daily yields, the weekly changes are positively autocorrelated, with a lag-one coefficient of 0.27: a move in the mortgage rate in one week tends to be followed by a move in the same direction the next, because the rate is a weekly survey average that adjusts to the bond market with a lag.











The effective Federal Funds Rate is monthly, from July 1954 to August 2023, 830 observations. It ranges from 0.05% in April 2020 to 19.10% in June 1981. The ADF statistic in levels is −3.18 with p = 0.091, which rejects at 10% but not at 5%, and the series is treated as I(1). The ACF at lag one is 0.99 and does not fall below 0.5 until lag 72, six years. After one difference the statistic is −8.41. The monthly changes have a lag-one autocorrelation of 0.39, the highest among the rate series, because the Fed moves the rate in sequences of steps in the same direction.











The Consumer Price Index is monthly, from January 1947 to August 2023, 920 observations, rising from 21.48 to 306.27. The series is seasonally adjusted at source. The ADF statistic in levels is −0.82 with p = 0.96, the weakest rejection in the table, as expected for a series that has risen in almost every month of the sample. After one difference the statistic is −5.43 and the unit root is rejected, but the differenced series has a lag-one autocorrelation of 0.59 and an ACF that decays slowly, since the monthly change in the index is inflation, and inflation is itself persistent. The ARMA section uses a second difference for this reason.











The unemployment rate is monthly, from January 1948 to August 2023, 908 observations, seasonally adjusted at source. It ranges from 2.5% in May 1953 to 14.7% in April 2020. The ADF statistic in levels is −3.92 with p = 0.013, so the unit root is rejected at the 5% level on the full sample. The ACF at lag one is 0.97 and falls below 0.5 at lag 17, faster than any other level series, which is consistent with a bounded series that returns toward a long-run rate. After one difference the statistic is −9.72 and the lag-one autocorrelation is 0.04.











Real GDP is quarterly, from the first quarter of 1947 to the second quarter of 2023, 306 observations, seasonally adjusted at source. It ranges from $2,172 billion in the third quarter of 1947 to $22,225 billion in the second quarter of 2023, in chained 2017 $. The ADF statistic in levels is −1.05 with p = 0.93. After one difference the statistic is −7.62 and the unit root is rejected. The lag-one autocorrelation of the differenced series is −0.12, so quarterly changes in the level are close to uncorrelated once the trend is removed. The ARMA section models the logarithm of the series.











The nominal broad dollar index is daily, from January 2006 to November 2023, 4,488 observations. It ranges from 85.47 on 26 July 2011 to 128.32 on 26 September 2022. The ADF statistic in levels is −2.71 with p = 0.28, so the unit root is not rejected. The ACF does not fall below 0.5 until lag 801, about three years. After one difference the statistic is −15.41 and the lag-one autocorrelation is 0.04. The financial time series section models the volatility of these daily changes.

Four of the identifiers end in FF. These are not Treasury yields. Each is the yield at that maturity minus the effective Federal Funds Rate on the same day, in % points. They are the inputs to the ARMA section and to the short-term visualizations, and, with the policy rate added back, they supply the short-maturity yields in the ARIMAX section’s yield-curve VAR. The DGS series are the yields themselves, at constant maturity, and cover the long end of the curve.

The series arrive at four frequencies. Treasury yields, the spreads, and the dollar index are daily, on Treasury market trading days. The mortgage rate is weekly, published on Thursdays. title: Conclusion
text:
I set out on a mission to understand how changes in the Federal Funds Rate, a key interest rate set by central banks, impact different parts of our economy. Using various complex models, I examined how the Federal Funds Rate changes affect things like government bond yields, our nation’s overall economic health (GDP), price changes (CPI), unemployment, home loan rates, and the strength of US dollar against other currencies.
My analysis began with a simple yet powerful idea: interest rates are like the engine’s throttle of the economy. When the central bank raises rates, it’s like pressing a brake pedal. This can slow down the economy, control rising prices (inflation), but also risk reducing business growth and increasing joblessness. On the other hand, lowering interest rates is like stepping on the gas pedal. It can speed up the economy and reduce unemployment but may also lead to too-high prices if not managed carefully.
Looking at the housing market, I found a direct connection to interest rate changes. Higher rates often cool down the housing market, making it more expensive for people to borrow money for homes. Lower rates do the opposite, making homes more affordable but potentially leading to too much borrowing and spending.
On a global scale, the strength of our dollar plays a big role. A strong dollar can be good for buying things from other countries but can make it harder for other countries to buy things from us. Economic crises, like the 2008 financial crisis or the COVID-19 pandemic, can cause big ups and downs in the dollar’s value, impacting global trade and investment.
One of the key things I learned was about the tricky balance between controlling inflation and keeping unemployment low. If the focus is too much on reducing inflation, it might increase unemployment. But if not enough attention is given to inflation, prices might rise too fast, affecting the stability of the economy.
Turning to GDP, I saw that its growth is a major sign of how well our economy is doing. A growing GDP usually means more jobs and better incomes, but it needs to be managed to avoid too much inflation or the risk of a recession.
The bond market, especially long-term bonds, gave me insights into what investors think will happen in the future. When central banks raise rates, these long-term yields often go up, as investors want more return on their investments due to expected inflation.
Looking at currency markets, I understood how the value of our dollar compared to other currencies indicates the health of the global economy. Changes in the dollar’s value can show how confident people are in the global economic situation and can be influenced by big economic events or crises.
Wrapping up my project, I realized how interconnected everything is — interest rates, inflation, unemployment, GDP growth, and currency markets. They all work together to shape our economic story. This journey through data and models not only improved my understanding but also showed the importance of careful and timely decisions in guiding our economy.
This analysis proves that understanding how monetary policy works and its effects is not just for academics; it’s crucial for everyone making decisions in our economy. Reflecting on my findings, I see the huge responsibility in balancing these different economic aspects to ensure a stable and prosperous future for us all.

What the Models Found
The four models agree on where the policy rate’s influence is direct and where it is not. In the Treasury market, the effect runs through the short end. The policy rate Granger-causes the 3-month, 6-month and 1-year yields and not the longer ones; the impulse responses show the 3-month yield moving three-quarters of the way with the policy rate on impact and nine-tenths after a year, while the 30-year moves a quarter on impact and a half after a year; and the single-equation regression puts the same-month pass-through to the 30-year yield at 0.13. Every yield Granger-causes the policy rate, which is the market anticipating the Federal Reserve. In the macroeconomy the policy rate Granger-causes output, prices, unemployment and the mortgage rate; a 0.9-point tightening shock lowers real GDP by half a percent over two to three years and raises unemployment by 0.16 points, with the mortgage rate absorbing about 40% of the move within two quarters.
The inflation regression is the model that did not find an effect, and the reason is instructive. The policy rate lagged a year has a coefficient indistinguishable from zero and adds nothing to inflation forecasts; the policy rate lagged a month has a positive, significant coefficient and makes the forecasts worse. Both results are what a reaction function produces. The Federal Reserve raises the rate when inflation is high, so the rate is correlated with inflation in the wrong direction for a causal reading and in a direction that does not survive out of sample. The VAR, which lets both variables respond to each other, finds that the policy rate Granger-causes prices, but its impulse response has the price level rising after a tightening, the price puzzle. The macroeconomic effect of policy on inflation is the one question in this section the data set cannot answer cleanly, because the system lacks the variable that would let it separate the Federal Reserve’s information from its action.


Model Choice
The regression form suits the 30-year yield and does not suit inflation. The Federal Reserve does not set the policy rate in response to the 30-year yield, so treating the policy rate as exogenous to it is a reasonable approximation at monthly frequency, and the estimated pass-through is the kind of quantity a regression can deliver. The Federal Reserve does set the policy rate in response to inflation, and a regression of inflation on the policy rate estimates that response as much as it estimates transmission. The twelve-month lag makes the regressor predetermined but cannot make it exogenous, since the rate a year ago responded to inflation a year ago, which is correlated with inflation today. For questions of effect, the VAR is the right instrument in this data set.
The two VARs are estimated in levels on series the exploratory analysis identified as I(1) with stationary spreads, that is, cointegrated. A levels VAR is consistent for the quantities used here, and imposing the cointegrating restrictions through a VECM would sharpen the long-horizon responses and the forecasts. Both selections settled on two lags, and in both the residuals are not fully white or the cross-validation prefers a simpler model, which is the usual position of a small VAR on fifty years of data that include several policy regimes. The macroeconomic VAR would be improved by a measure of expected inflation or commodity prices, which is how the price puzzle is normally resolved.


Forecasting
None of the four models forecasts well far ahead, and none should be expected to. The inflation model forecasts 4.5% for the year from September 2023, carrying forward the 2021–2023 persistence, against 3.6% in the year before. The 30-year model has no information beyond two months once the policy rate is held fixed. The yield-curve VAR beats a random walk by 6% one step ahead and 2% at a year, entirely at the short end. The macroeconomic VAR’s policy-rate forecasts were worse than a random walk over 2007–2023, and its eight-quarter projection, a policy rate of 2.9%, unemployment at 5.6% and flat real GDP, should be read as the pattern of a typical easing cycle in the sample rather than a prediction.


Limitations
The findings rest on Granger causality and orthogonalised impulse responses, both of which identify effects from the ordering of variables in time and within the period, not from any measure of the Federal Reserve’s intentions. The yield-curve VAR uses the effective rate, which moved with the target during the 1982–2008 period and sat at the floor of the target range from 2009 to 2015 and 2020 to 2022; a VAR on that sample treats a rate the Federal Reserve could not lower as an ordinary observation. The short-maturity yields are reconstructed from spreads and differ from the published constant-maturity yields by the averaging convention. The macroeconomic VAR has five variables and 209 quarters; with two lags each equation has 11 coefficients, which is adequate, but the bootstrap bands are wide at long horizons, and the cross-validation on the post-2007 period shows the estimated dynamics do not hold at the zero bound.
